hook

This cheese sandwich cost twelve thousand dollars. It was served at what was supposed to be the party of the century. A private island in the Bahamas. Supermodels. Private jets. Luxury villas. The biggest stars in music. Thousands of people paid a fortune to be there. But when they landed, the villas did not exist. The stars were gone. Just rain-soaked disaster tents, and this sad cheese sandwich, that the whole world laughed at. So how did a twenty-five year old convince the entire internet to buy a festival that was never real? This is the story of Fyre Festival.
billy

New York. Billy McFarland was a young entrepreneur with big dreams, and an even bigger mouth. At twenty-two, he launched a members-only card for rich young people, promising exclusive parties and VIP access. He loved the lifestyle. Fast cars, fancy dinners, and always the next big idea. And his next idea would make him famous, for all the wrong reasons.
app

He teamed up with the rapper Ja Rule. Together, they built an app called Fyre, to let anyone book celebrities for their parties. To make the app famous, Billy came up with a wild plan. They would throw a music festival, on an island, so exclusive and so beautiful that everyone on earth would be talking about it.
promo

They flew the biggest supermodels in the world to a beach in the Bahamas. Bella Hadid. Emily Ratajkowski. Hailey Baldwin. They filmed them on yachts, swimming with pigs, dancing on white sand. The video looked like paradise. Then, on one single day, hundreds of influencers posted the exact same thing on Instagram. A simple orange square. No details. Just mystery. Kendall Jenner was reportedly paid two hundred and fifty thousand dollars for one post. One single post.
tickets

And it worked like magic. Tickets went from about five hundred dollars, all the way up to twelve thousand dollars for a VIP package. People were promised luxury villas, private jet flights from Miami, and meals made by famous chefs, and a lineup with Blink one eighty two, Migos and Major Lazer. Thousands of people bought in. Everyone wanted to be there. There was just one tiny detail nobody knew.
problems

There was no festival. Billy had sold a dream before building anything. They lost their first island, after breaking a promise to its owners. With only a few weeks left, they moved to a bare gravel lot on another island. No water system. No toilets. No houses. Nothing. Experts told Billy it was impossible. So what did he do? He kept selling tickets anyway.
money

Behind the scenes, the money was running out fast. To keep going, Billy borrowed millions of dollars, and lied to investors about how much the company was really making. Local Bahamian workers built day and night, often without being paid. And the luxury villas? They were never built. Instead, Billy bought hundreds of disaster relief tents. And then, the guests arrived.
arrival

April twenty seventh, twenty seventeen. The first planes landed. Guests in their best festival outfits stepped onto buses, ready for paradise. What they found looked like a disaster zone. Soaking wet mattresses. Piles of luggage dumped in the dark. And the headliners? Blink one eighty two had already pulled out. There wasn't even a stage. But the moment that ended it all was still to come.
sandwich

Dinner time. Instead of gourmet meals, guests got two slices of bread, two slices of cheese, and a sad little salad in a foam box. One guest took a photo, and posted it. Within hours, that cheese sandwich went around the world. The internet could not stop laughing. Guests rushed back to the airport, and some were stuck there for hours. The next morning, Fyre Festival was officially cancelled.
fall

The fallout was huge. Lawsuits poured in, worth millions of dollars. Local workers and businesses were left unpaid. One Bahamian restaurant owner, Maryann Rolle, used about fifty thousand dollars of her own savings to pay her staff. In twenty eighteen, Billy pleaded guilty to fraud. Investors had lost around twenty-six million dollars. And here's the crazy part. While he was out on bail, he ran another ticket scam. He was sentenced to six years in prison.
end

In twenty nineteen, two documentaries about the disaster came out, and millions of people watched. Billy was released in twenty twenty-two. And then, believe it or not, he announced Fyre Festival Two. So how did he fool the whole internet? With beautiful videos, famous faces, and one orange square. The man who sold paradise proved that a perfect post can sell anything. Even a party that never existed. If you want more crazy true stories like this one, subscribe to Rise and Ruin.
